turn_annotations.result: The tutor's strategy does not seem to be effective yet because the tutor spends 20 minutes of the tutoring session on a very worthwhile problem set containing lots of important math concepts, and then does not review it at all to see how the student did.  It seems unusual to not gather the information from the student, especially if the student took longer than expected to complete the work and struggled on at least two problems that we know about.  Having taught 6th grade math before, I would be concerned about fact fluency and pace of work completion if it took a student 20 minutes to complete this particular problem set, unless there was a situation where the student had a processing or learning difference that prevented them from working at a typical pace.  These 15 problems could mostly be done with quick mental math, so I was surprised to see the student took the full 20 minutes.  It seems like it would be well worth the tutor's and student's time to take a few minutes to review the problems, have the student explain their thinking, and reteach concepts that the student needed help with.  However, it is important to note that the tutor immediately goes into a well-scaffolded lesson on what algebra is, what variables are, and how to solve for a variable, so it seems that the tutor is addressing the student's misconceptions.  With that assistance, the student begins to demonstrate better understanding and quicker work completion.  I still think it would be worthwhile for the tutor to see how the student did on these 15 problems so that the tutor will know which concepts they need to review and/or reteach with the student.
